solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: One in no hurry to whizz round north

indicators.note: the sailing word goes round the compass letter, enclosing it

parts.note: to sail is to move along swiftly and smoothly
N is the compass abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: Someone is urged to race around the northern part of town, though they are in no rush.
explanation.definitionFit: The garden mollusc is proverbially slow, so it is a creature never in a hurry.

clue.text: Impressed by English dash

parts.note: to stamp is to impress a mark on something

explanation.surface: Someone is impressed by an English sprint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impressed' looks like admiration but is a mark pressed into a surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A stampede is a sudden mass rush, a headlong dash of animals or people.

clue.text: Weapon found in famous school in East End

indicators.note: Cockneys of London's East End drop their aitches, so the opening H goes

parts.note: Harrow is a famous English public school in north-west London

explanation.surface: A weapon is discovered at a well-known school in London's East End.
explanation.walkthrough: East End Cockney speech drops the H sound, so HARROW said that way loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An arrow is the missile shot from a bow, one of the oldest weapons.

clue.text: Romeo appearing in tatty denim, alas

indicators.note: tatty means worn and messed up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A would-be lover shows up in shabby jeans, sadly.
explanation.definitionFit: A Romeo, after Shakespeare's lover, is a womaniser who charms the opposite sex.

clue.text: Poor man's university featuring in the Sun?

indicators.note: the university letter appears inside the newspaper word

parts.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper, an example of a paper, hence the question mark

explanation.surface: A tabloid story about a penniless man's college days.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is a British tabloid, so it stands for PAPER by example; the question mark flags that.
explanation.definitionFit: A pauper is someone destitute, a person with no money at all.

clue.text: Head of ambassadorial party making trouble

indicators.note: head of means the first letter of the following word

parts.note: only its opening letter is used; that the answer also sits inside this word is a coincidence
a do is an informal word for a party or celebration

explanation.surface: The chief diplomat's reception is stirring up difficulties.
explanation.definitionFit: Ado means fuss or bother, as in much ado about nothing.

clue.text: Bridge? It's a card game

definitions.meaning: a floating structure of boats or drums forms a temporary bridge; the question mark marks the card-game false lead
a British gambling game in which players aim for a total of twenty-one, like blackjack

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether bridge is the card game in question.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bridge' pretends to be the card game, but the first sense is a floating crossing.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a floating crossing on boats and the British name for blackjack.

clue.text: Ruminants heading north for grass

indicators.note: in a down clue going north means reading from bottom to top

parts.note: deer are cud-chewing animals, ruminants

explanation.surface: Grazing animals head north in search of pasture.
explanation.definitionFit: A reed is a tall grass that grows in marshes and wet ground.

clue.text: Notice manner in which chess game may end?

definitions.meaning: handing in your notice means formally quitting a job

definitions.text: manner in which chess game may end?
definitions.meaning: a player in a lost position may concede by toppling the king rather than play on

explanation.surface: Someone observes how a game of chess might finish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notice' looks like a verb meaning observe; it is the noun, a letter quitting a job.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both quitting a post and conceding a lost game in chess.

clue.text: Badger I treated for cut

indicators.note: letters that are treated are processed into a new form, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A badger, having been patched up by a vet, has a wound.
explanation.definitionFit: To abridge a text is to shorten it, trimming it down to fewer words.

clue.text: Zoo unceremoniously caging leopard

indicators.note: the words hold the answer inside them as a cage holds an animal

explanation.surface: A zoo bundles a big cat into a cage without any ceremony.
explanation.definitionFit: The ounce is another name for the snow leopard of Central Asian mountains.

clue.text: Initially politician easily wins seat

indicators.note: initially means take the opening letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: A politician comfortably wins a parliamentary seat.
explanation.definitionFit: A pew is a long bench for sitting in church, so a kind of seat.

clue.text: Leak from European delegation

parts.note: a mission is a group of people sent abroad to represent a country

explanation.surface: A story was leaked by a delegation from Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: A leak of gas or fumes is a discharge, which is what an emission is.

clue.text: Barely enter the water?

parts.note: barely suggests a tentative toe in the water, but read it as nakedly: going swimming bare

explanation.surface: Someone only just dips into the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barely' seems to mean only just, but here means without clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: To go swimming naked is the activity described, with barely read as bare of clothing.

clue.text: Set off round lake, a little frightened

indicators.note: the setting-off word goes round the lake letter

parts.note: to start is to set off on a journey
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: Someone set off around a lake, slightly scared.
explanation.definitionFit: Being startled is a brief jolt of alarm, a mild fright rather than terror.

clue.text: Keep quiet about sex? No problem

definitions.meaning: it is a familiar euphemism for sex, so this tells you not to bring it up
a polite reply to someone thanking you, meaning it was no trouble

explanation.surface: Someone asked to stay silent about intimate matters breezily agrees.
explanation.walkthrough: IT as slang for sex is old British usage (as in 'having it'); read the phrase literally and it becomes an instruction to stay silent on the subject.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a stock reply to thanks, saying the favour was no trouble at all.

clue.text: Put an end to fun frolicking with Lily

indicators.note: frolicking means romping about, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A spoilsport puts a stop to Lily's playful amusement.
explanation.definitionFit: To nullify is to cancel or invalidate, so bring something to an end.

clue.text: Tiny creatures of the deep, a hundred on board

indicators.note: the hundred goes after, as if placed on, the board

parts.note: a plank is a long flat piece of timber, a board
a ton is informal British for a hundred (runs, miles per hour, pounds)

explanation.surface: Marine creatures in their hundreds are hauled aboard a ship.
explanation.definitionFit: Plankton are the minute organisms drifting in seas and lakes, the tiny life of the ocean.

clue.text: My dog's had a heart transplant!

indicators.note: the middle letter of the dog word is swapped out for another letter, a new heart

parts.note: a cur is a mongrel dog

explanation.surface: An astonished owner exclaims that their pet has undergone cardiac surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle letter of CUR is replaced by O; 'My' is not a possessive here but an exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are British exclamations of surprise, like 'gosh' or 'wow'.

clue.text: Country that's cold, by all accounts

indicators.note: accounts are reports people give out loud, so this signals a word that sounds alike

parts.note: chilly means cold

explanation.surface: A nation is reported to be chilly.
explanation.definitionFit: Chile is a long narrow South American nation on the Pacific coast.

clue.text: Report left in toilet

indicators.note: the left letter is placed inside the toilet word

parts.note: bog is British slang for a toilet

explanation.surface: A document was abandoned in the lavatory.
explanation.walkthrough: BOG is everyday British slang for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: A blog is an online journal in which someone writes up and reports events.

clue.text: Scottish landowner, one wreathed in fat

indicators.note: the numeral is surrounded by the fat word, as by a wreath

parts.note: lard is pig fat used in cooking
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A portly Scottish estate owner is described as swathed in fat.
explanation.definitionFit: A laird is the Scots term for the owner of a landed estate.

clue.text: Cut out adviser every now and then

indicators.note: occasionally, so take every other letter of the word

explanation.surface: A counsellor is dropped from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking the second, fourth and sixth letters of 'adviser' gives D, I, E.
explanation.definitionFit: An engine that cuts out stops suddenly, and is said to have died.

clue.text: Ancient advertisement for the police

parts.note: ancient means old
a bill is a printed poster advertising something

explanation.surface: An old poster appealing for police recruits.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Bill is British slang for the police force.

clue.text: It's a hot spring, man said

indicators.note: said means the word for man is spoken, giving a word that sounds like it

parts.note: a geezer is British slang for a man or bloke

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a spring is warm.
explanation.walkthrough: GEEZER is London slang for a bloke; in British speech it sounds like GEYSER.
explanation.definitionFit: A geyser is a natural spring that shoots up jets of hot water and steam.

clue.text: Beg Penny to go first

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for a penny in British money
to lead is to go in front of everyone else

explanation.surface: Someone implores a girl called Penny to take the first turn.
explanation.definitionFit: To plead is to ask earnestly, much as to entreat or implore.
